solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Male raccoon originally from part of N Africa

indicators.note: the letters of the word are taken back to some other original order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A male raccoon's origins are traced to North Africa, though raccoons are American animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' signals an anagram: RACCOON is rearranged to ORACCON after M.
explanation.definitionFit: Morocco lies in the north-west of Africa, so someone or something from there is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Small county? Italian finds room to live in

parts.note: Beds is the short form of Bedfordshire, an English county, so a 'small' (abbreviated) county

explanation.surface: An Italian moving to a little English county finds somewhere to live.
explanation.walkthrough: BEDS is the abbreviation for Bedfordshire, a county north of London; 'Small' hints at the shortened name.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsit is a single rented room used for both sleeping and living, common in British cities.

clue.text: Question, one holding EU up repeatedly: no good waiting patiently?

indicators.note: Q and I hold something between them, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: the reversed pair is written out twice in a row
in a down clue, up means the letters are read bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about the EU, with a sigh that waiting patiently does no good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses EU, as this is a down clue, and 'repeatedly' doubles the result; 'holding' puts it between Q and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing in line is the British way of waiting one's turn patiently; the question mark marks it as a description by example.

clue.text: Cockney's custom? To an extent

indicators.note: a Cockney, a working-class Londoner, traditionally drops the H sound at the start of words

parts.note: a habit is a custom or usual practice

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Cockney has a custom, answered with a guarded 'somewhat'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cockney's' tells you to drop the initial H, as Cockney (East London) speech does: HABIT becomes ABIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is 'a bit' so means it is so slightly or partly, the same hedge as to some degree.

clue.text: Engineers to drink a French wine, gorge

indicators.note: RE takes the other letters into itself, as a drinker takes in wine

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
vin is the French word for wine

explanation.surface: Army engineers sit down to drink French wine and gorge themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gorge' looks like a verb about overeating, but it is the noun, a deep valley.
explanation.definitionFit: A ravine is a narrow, steep-sided valley, exactly what a gorge is in geography.

clue.text: Yours truly twice passed on cultural motif

indicators.note: the word for the speaker is written out two times

parts.note: 'yours truly' is a jokey way for the speaker to say me

explanation.surface: The writer has twice handed down some cultural motif.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Dawkins coined the term for an idea or behaviour spread from person to person through imitation, a cultural unit passed on.

clue.text: Spaniard perhaps turning in late, so jaded

indicators.note: turning says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Spaniard, maybe, turning in for the night late and weary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the hidden-word signal the draft left unmarked: ESOJ sits inside 'latE SO Jaded', and 'turning' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: José is a very common Spanish first name, so it stands for a Spaniard by example, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Fair representation of Buendias

indicators.note: a representation re-presents the letters of the name in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A fair portrait of the Buendía family from One Hundred Years of Solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: The Buendías are the family in García Márquez's novel, theme of this puzzle (the setter's name, Aureliano, is one of them).
explanation.definitionFit: Being impartial and fair means having no bias towards either side.

clue.text: Hour on and off to go round on quiet Japanese island

indicators.note: the picked letters split to surround the rest
taking letters on and off means every other letter of the word Hour

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: An hour on and off, circling quietly round a Japanese island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on and off' takes alternate letters of Hour; 'to go round' wraps those two letters around the rest. Both 'on's work: one in the indicator, one as a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Honshu is the largest of Japan's main islands, home to Tokyo.

clue.text: Worked hard to initially install light

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of install is used

parts.note: an LED is a light-emitting diode, a small light

explanation.surface: Someone worked hard to fit a new light.
explanation.definitionFit: To toil is to labour long and hard, so the past tense matches having worked hard.

clue.text: Small infant's bed for bairn?

definitions.note: a bairn is a child in Scotland, so a bairn is likely to be one of its people

parts.note: a cot is a baby's bed with high sides

explanation.surface: A little cot for a Scottish baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bairn' is Scots for child; the question mark says a bairn is just one example of a person from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A child born in Scotland is a native of that country, the question mark marking the example.

clue.text: Safely secured fixing eg in bath

indicators.note: fixing as in rigging or rearranging, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something like fixing a fitting in the bath is now safely done.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In the bag' is an idiom for something as good as won or certain, safely secured.

clue.text: With intention of studying, or becoming bullfighter

parts.note: to, as in 'in order to', expresses intention
to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: Choosing between going to study or becoming a bullfighter.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you 'read' a subject at university, meaning study it.
explanation.definitionFit: A toreador is a bullfighter, especially one on horseback in older usage.

clue.text: Virtually the same, morally?

definitions.meaning: practically, almost, as in 'it is all but finished'
equal in goodness, read literally as matching someone in virtue

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means practically, and taken literally it says equally good, the same in moral worth.

clue.text: Put at risk, cease to be annoyed?

parts.note: to end something is to cease it
anger is the state of being annoyed, so stopping it is ceasing to be annoyed

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether calming down could ever put someone at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads cryptically: END + ANGER is to stop being cross.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger someone is to expose them to harm or danger.

clue.text: Sam Dee, flustered, cancels

indicators.note: someone flustered is in a muddle, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A flustered Sam Dee calls something off.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a will's gift is adeemed when it is revoked or cancelled, often because the item no longer exists.

clue.text: Spurs? We can have them for breakfast!

definitions.meaning: urges on, as in egging someone on

definitions.text: We can have them for breakfast!
definitions.meaning: boiled, fried or scrambled, a breakfast staple

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurs' tempts as Tottenham Hotspur, the London football club; it is the verb meaning urges.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg on is to urge or spur someone, and hens' produce is a classic breakfast food.

clue.text: Lands in bottom of hole, say

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Something drops and lands at the bottom of a hole, so to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land or property owned by one person, so it means lands.

clue.text: Show: a seaside attraction from what we are told

indicators.note: what we are told is heard, so the words are spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a pier is a classic attraction at a British seaside resort

explanation.surface: A show by the sea, going by what people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pier' spoken sounds like the answer; piers with arcades are a fixture of British seaside towns.
explanation.definitionFit: To show up or turn up somewhere is to appear, as a verb.

clue.text: Storyline's particular lack of theme, first of all

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the noun storyline is followed by a verb linking it to the wordplay; the definition itself is just the noun

indicators.note: first of all means the opening letter of every following word

explanation.surface: A storyline has a peculiar lack of any theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storyline's' is 'storyline is'; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A story's sequence of events is its main narrative thread, a synonym for storyline.

clue.text: Violent diatribe coming from Amaranta

indicators.note: the letters come out of the middle of the name

explanation.surface: An angry tirade from Amaranta, a fiery woman in One Hundred Years of Solitude.
explanation.definitionFit: A rant is a long, loud, angry speech, a fierce tirade.

clue.text: Garcia Marquez, for one, nevertheless bathed in aura endlessly

indicators.note: the short word for though is placed inside, surrounded as if bathed
endlessly means the last letter of aura is dropped

parts.note: tho, short for though, means nevertheless

explanation.surface: García Márquez, for all that, glows in an aura of greatness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the last letter of aura; 'bathed in' puts the informal spelling of though inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriel García Márquez wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Soldier married in Macondo originally

indicators.note: the letters return to some original order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier first married in Macondo, the novel's fictional town.
explanation.walkthrough: Macondo is the town in One Hundred Years of Solitude; 'originally' signals rearranging M with MACONDO.
explanation.definitionFit: A commando is a soldier trained for raids, so a type of soldier.

clue.text: Getting warmer Thursday: not half warm, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the letters are reversed
only the first half of the word warm is kept

explanation.surface: A forecast that Thursday will get warmer, though only half as warm as hoped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' leaves WA from warm; 'on reflection' turns it to AW.
explanation.definitionFit: A thaw is a period of warmer weather when ice and snow melt.
